data.title: Bitget to discontinue services for some users in one-off exercise
data.description:
Bitget said it will discontinue services for some crypto users in a one-off exercise

The cryptocurrency exchange said in a post on X on Saturday that users’ funds will remain safe during the service change for certain customers, while its crypto platform continues to operate.

Users can verify the safety of their assets here: https://abcdstable.com/academy/how-to-verify-your-assets-in-bitget.

The users in question will receive direct notifications by email, in-app messages and/or push notifications about the next steps, relevant deadlines and arrangements for withdrawal. Users who have not received official notifications from Bitget can continue to use their accounts as usual.

The Bitget customer support team can assist with pending orders, withdrawals and other account-related questions throughout the process. The exchange reminded users to use only official channels and to be cautious of phishing links, impersonation accounts and unverified information.

Cointelegraph reported on Sept. 25 that Bitget had confirmed unauthorized transfers and temporarily suspended withdrawals as it investigated a security breach. The total stolen in the breach amounted to about $388 million, a security company said later.

data.title: China AI supply-chain IPOs hold firm despite valuation pullback, Citi says
data.description:
By Selena Li

Listings of Chinese AI supply chain companies are expected to stand their ground weathering rising valuation concerns and increasingly sharper scrutiny, a Citi banker working with Chinese companies said.

  • Despite recent valuation pullbacks on data centre companies, largely originating from the US market, future AI supply-chain listings would continue in Hong Kong, said Simon Yuen, Citi's head of China investment banking.

  • Chinese companies plan to list in Hong Kong are cushioned by a roughly even split between domestic Chinese and international demand, Yuen, who also heads Citi’s financial institutions group in APAC, said ​on the sidelines of the IMF meetings in Bangkok.

  • The market is supported by a pool of local liquidity, with rising southbound capital from the Chinese mainland emerging as a key buying force, Yuen said.

  • Still, "if the whole AI cycle turns in the US — and we have seen some volatility in the last few weeks — you will see an impact everywhere, Hong Kong included,” he warned.

  • Many Chinese hardware players have proactively established manufacturing footprints outside mainland China, he said, which helps them better service global clients and mitigate geopolitical friction.

  • Chinese hardware suppliers have benefited from the global AI infrastructure boom, gaining both sales volume growth and higher unit prices, Yuen said.

  • Next year, the focus in Hong Kong's equity capital markets is expected to shift away from pure hardware, toward Chinese artificial intelligence models and application developers, he said.

  • "But these companies need to have a proven business model. They need to show very strong growth and profitability," he said.

  • Propelled by Chinese tech funding demand, 118 firms went public in Hong Kong in the first nine months of the year, raising HK$388 billion ($49.4 billion), up 106% year-on-year.

($1 = 7.8479 Hong Kong dollars)

data.title: Ixigo Q2 results: Online travel platform swings to profit at ₹61 crore; revenue rises 13%
data.description:
Le Travenues Technology, the parent company of online travel platform Ixigo, reported a consolidated net profit of ₹61.3 crore for the September quarter, compared with a net loss of ₹3.2 crore in the year-ago period.

Revenue from operations rose 12.9% year-on-year to ₹321 crore in Q2FY27, compared with ₹284.2 crore in the corresponding quarter last year.

Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) stood at ₹18.1 crore, compared with an EBITDA loss of ₹3.7 crore a year earlier.

Among its business segments, train revenue rose to ₹149.14 crore in Q2FY27 from ₹128.11 crore a year earlier, while bus revenue increased to ₹81.04 crore from ₹65.41 crore. Flight revenue, however, declined to ₹82.66 crore from ₹89.39 crore.

The company also reported an exceptional gain of ₹40.66 crore following the reduction of its stake in Freshbus Private Limited, which ceased to be an associate in August 2026.

For the first half of FY27, revenue from operations increased to ₹677.71 crore from ₹600.28 crore in the year-ago period, while consolidated net profit rose to ₹97.66 crore from ₹15.48 crore.

Shares of the Le Travenues Technology closed nearly 6% higher at ₹145.98 on Friday ahead of the results announcement. The stock has fallen more than 39% so far in 2026 and 56% over the last 12 months.

data.title: JSW Steel: NCLT approves merger of Piombino Steel with parent company
data.description:
The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), Mumbai Bench, has approved the amalgamation of Piombino Steel Limited with JSW Steel, paving the way for the consolidation of the two entities.

In a regulatory filing on Saturday, October 17, JSW Steel said the tribunal pronounced its order on October 16. The scheme will become effective once the companies file the certified order with the Registrar of Companies, Mumbai. The appointed date for the merger is January 1, 2026.

The merger is aimed at aligning JSW Steel’s long-term strategic interests by enabling it to directly hold its investment in Bhushan Power and Steel Limited (BPSL). According to the scheme, this would facilitate transactions and investments related to BPSL’s business without the involvement of minority shareholders.

The consolidation is also expected to provide JSW Steel with additional cash to fund its growth plans, reduce the number of entities and regulatory compliances, and lower administrative and overhead costs. It is expected to simplify financial consolidation and eliminate duplication in record-keeping and management functions.

Under the share-swap arrangement, shareholders of Piombino Steel will receive 10 fully paid-up equity shares of JSW Steel, with a face value of ₹1 each, for every 156 fully paid-up equity shares of Piombino Steel, with a face value of ₹10 each.

The NCLT order directs the companies to file a certified copy of the order and the scheme with the Registrar of Companies within 30 days of receiving the order. Piombino Steel will be dissolved without winding up following the amalgamation.

The scheme was approved by 94.86% of the valid votes cast by JSW Steel shareholders and 97.20% of the valid votes cast by public shareholders, according to the tribunal order. The Regional Director, Western Region, had raised no objections to the scheme.

JSW Steel is engaged in the production and sale of steel and allied products in India and global markets, while Piombino Steel operates in the trading and dealing of steel and allied products, iron ore, coal, coke, minerals and metal scrap.

Shares of JSW Steel closed 1.3% higher ₹1,216.30 on Friday ahead of the announcement. The stock has advanced about 4% so far this year.

data.title: Trump Denies SpaceX’s Starlink Was Slowed Down Over Ukraine By Either White House Or Elon Musk: Report
data.description:
Key points:
  • Asked by reporters who was responsible for pausing access to Starlink for the Ukrainian military, President Donald Trump denied that either he or Musk was behind the move, according to a CNBC report.
  • SpaceX CEO Elon Musk had previously sought to distance himself from direct responsibility, saying that Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government.
  • Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Friday that Starlink was not completely shut down in Ukraine but that its speed had been reduced.

President Donald Trump on Friday denied that either the White House or Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (SPCX) CEO Elon Musk ordered restrictions on Starlink satellite internet services used by Ukraine’s armed forces.

The comments come after Ukrainian officials said the restrictions disrupted military operations and the country’s ability to intercept Russian attacks. Musk, meanwhile, had previously pointed responsibility toward the U.S. government, while conflicting reports have emerged over who ordered the slowdown.

SpaceX shares fell nearly 2% during the regular trading session on Friday, and declined 0.4% further in the after-hours trade.

Trump Denies Ordering Starlink Restrictions

Asked by reporters in Washington who was responsible for pausing access to Starlink for the Ukrainian military, Trump denied that either he or Musk was behind the move, according to a report by CNBC.

“Well, I don’t know if it was anybody because it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” Trump said. “And from what I understand, it’s the same as it’s always been.”

The denial follows reports pointing in different directions. Reuters reported Thursday, citing two U.S. officials, that the call to restrict Starlink in Ukraine came from the White House, although the report did not identify who made the order.

The Telegraph, meanwhile, reported Friday that Musk had “approached” Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink in Ukraine and that they both played a role in imposing the restrictions.

Musk had previously sought to distance himself from direct responsibility, writing on X that Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government.

The conflicting accounts come amid heightened tensions between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy over Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil infrastructure.

Zelenskyy Says Starlink Was Slowed, Not Shut Off

Zelenskyy said in a post on X on Friday that Starlink was not completely shut down in Ukraine but that its speed had been reduced, with the restrictions having significant consequences for Ukrainian military operations.

According to Zelenskyy, the slowdown affected Ukraine’s ability to use Starlink-connected systems to intercept Russian drones attacking civilians. He said Ukrainian forces also rely on the service for mid-range strikes against Russian military targets in occupied Ukrainian territory.

“We couldn’t use a tool that helps protect people. That’s very painful and frustrating,” he added.

Zelenskyy also said the restrictions affected frontline logistics, including drones used to deliver food and water to Ukrainian soldiers. He said the service had begun to recover but had not yet returned completely to its previous performance.

What Retail Investors Think Of SPCX Stock

Retail sentiment on Stocktwits around SpaceX trended in the ‘bearish’ territory at the time of writing.

SPCX stock is down 3% year-to-date. The S&P 500 ETF (SPY) is up 16% over the past 12 months, while the Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF (VTI) is up 15%.

data.title: Former Deputy PM LK Advani hospitalised with chest infection, condition stable: Apollo Hospitals
data.description:
New Delhi, Oct. 17 -- Veteran Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leader and former Deputy Prime Minister Lal Krishna Advani has been admitted to Apollo Hospitals in New Delhi with a chest infection, the hospital said on Saturday.

Advani is currently in the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) under the care of Dr Vinit Suri, Senior Consultant - Neurology.

His condition is stable, and he remains under close medical observation, the hospital said.

Advani, one of the senior-most leaders of the BJP, has played a significant role in Indian politics over several decades.

His hospitalisation has prompted messages of concern and wishes for his speedy recovery from political leaders across the country.

Earlier in the day, Union Health Minister JP Nadda visited Advani at Apollo Hospital and enquired about his health.

Kanak Vardhan Singh Deo, Deputy Chief Minister of Odisha, expressed concern over Advani's hospitalisation and extended his wishes for the veteran leader's recovery in a post on X.

"Deeply concerned to learn of the hospitalisation of our revered statesman, senior BJP leader and former Deputy Prime Minister, Shri Lal Krishna Advani Ji, due to a chest infection. May Mahaprabhu Shri Jagannath bestow upon him strength, resilience, and swift recovery, so that he may continue to inspire the nation with his wisdom and guidance," Odisha deputy CM wrote.

Advani is regarded as one of the prominent figures in the BJP's political history and has held several key positions during his long public career, including serving as India's Deputy Prime Minister.

Nadda's visit to the hospital reflects the concern among party leaders regarding Advani's health.

As the 98-year-old continues to receive medical care, his supporters and well-wishers are hoping for his recovery. His reported stable condition has offered reassurance amid concerns surrounding his hospitalisation.

data.title: Robotics Remains In Its ‘Lego Era,’ Says Former Nvidia Leader Turned VC as Physical AI Awaits Its ChatGPT Moment
data.description:
Robotics remains in a "Lego era," with actuators, robotic hands, software, and safety standards still being rebuilt, and not on the cusp of a ChatGPT moment even as capital floods into AI. Amulya Vishwanath, founder of Techable VC and a former NVIDIA Corp. product marketing leader, made the case on TechCrunch’s Equity podcast that aired on Friday.

Vishwanath spent seven years leading product marketing for Nvidia’s robotics platforms. She also worked on the company’s Isaac Lab and the GR00T humanoid effort.

Simulation, Safety Seen as Next Catalysts

"There’s been quite a bit of progress. But that said, there’s a Lego era that’s happening for robotics," she said, adding that simulation will grow more critical.

Vishwanath said the industry needs "more emphasis on open-source safety and newer standards" that need to be set for robotics. Large companies now partner with startups and universities, she added, citing a possible tie-up among NVIDIA, a university, startups and companies.

Early Money Goes to the Building Blocks

That view shapes where Vishwanath invests. Her firm backs early-stage startups in robotics, materials science and life sciences, where the foundational pieces are still being built.

Views differ on how close deployment is. Ouster Inc. CEO Angus Pacala told Benzinga in August that mature pilots are moving into production, but the key question is whether robots can work safely every day for years.

A September Citrini Research report found most humanoid robots remain in development, training or tele-operated demos, with real-world deployments closer to pilots than clear return-on-investment cases.

That gap explains her focus on components. Vishwanath said U.S. startups are now making actuators, robotic hands and U.S.-made robots, and she called a domestic supply chain important.

Actuators act as a robot’s muscles, and a single humanoid needs dozens.

data.title: Financial Services Institutions Bureau to be headed by SCL Das, former Secretary, MSME Ministry
data.description:
The Government has nominated seven members, including Subhas Chandra Lal Das, former Secretary, MSME Ministry; Arijit Basu, former Managing Director, State Bank of India; and Satish K Marathe, former Director, Central Board of the Reserve Bank of India, to the Financial Services Institutions Bureau (FSIB).

Lal, who is also Chairman of the Delhi Electricity Regulatory Commission, has been appointed as Part-Time Chairman of FSIB.

Besides Basu and Marathe, other Members of the Bureau include R Subramanian, former Executive Director, RBI; Siddhartha Mohanty former CEO & MD, Life Insurance Corporation of India; Neeja Kapur, former Chairman & Managing Director, New India Assurance Co. Ltd; and T. L. Alamelu, former Whole-Time Member (Non-Life), Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India.

The aforementioned appointment are for a period of three years, with effect from the date of notification of this resolution, or until further orders, whichever is earlier.

In 2022, the Central Government constituted the FSIB for the purpose of recommending persons for appointment as whole-time directors and non-executive chairpersons on the Boards of Directors in Public Sector Banks, financial institutions and Public Sector Insurers.

FSIB’s mandate includes advising the Government on matters relating to appointments, transfer or extension of term of office and termination of services of the said directors; advise the Government on the desired management structure at the Board level for PSBs, FIs and PSIs; build a databank containing data related to the performance of PSBs, FIs and PSIs; among others.

data.title: Trump Waives Russia Energy Tariffs, Sanctions A Week After Diesel Deal As Crude Oil Prices Soar To A 5-Month High
data.description:
Key points:
  • The Graham Act, signed into law on Sept. 18, authorized sanctions, restrictions and duties targeting Russia and certain foreign persons and countries.
  • The law also allows the president to waive those measures if he certifies to Congress that doing so is in the national interest of the U.S.
  • Trump’s Oct. 16 executive order invokes that authority, stating that he has submitted the required certification and report to Congress.

President Donald Trump has waived the application of new Russia-related sanctions and tariffs authorized under the recently enacted Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act.

The waiver, issued Friday, comes less than a month after Trump signed the Graham Act into law and about a week after the administration’s diesel deal with Russia.

Trump Waives New Russia Tariffs

The Graham Act, signed into law on Sept. 18, authorized sanctions, restrictions and duties targeting Russia and certain foreign persons and countries. The law also allows the president to waive those measures if he certifies to Congress that doing so is in the national interest of the U.S.

Trump’s Oct. 16 executive order invokes that authority, stating that he has submitted the required certification and report to Congress. The president waived the application of duties provided under key sections of the Graham Act, as well as several sanctions and restrictions targeting foreign persons.

However, the order leaves a framework in place for potentially steep tariffs on Russian goods and countries that continue to buy Russian energy or facilitate sanctions evasion.

The waiver will remain in effect until Trump or the Secretary of State, in consultation with other senior officials, determines that further action is appropriate.

Existing Russia-related sanctions imposed under earlier executive orders have been kept in place.

Trump Sets Up Sweeping Russia Tariff Structure

Trump’s executive order also laid out a sweeping tariff structure that could be activated against Russia and countries involved in Russian energy trade.

The order calls for a 500% ad valorem duty on goods from Russia, subject to exceptions in the Graham Act and the waivers issued by Trump.

It also provides for an additional 100% tariff on goods from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil and natural gas if those countries knowingly make new purchases of Russian-origin crude or natural gas on or after Oct. 18.

The order directs the U.S. Trade Representative, working with the State, Treasury and Energy departments, to monitor Russian oil and gas purchases and sanctions evasion and regularly report developments to Trump.

Crude Oil Prices Hit Five-Month High

Crude oil prices rose last week, with the U.S. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures expiring in November rising 10.88% to $101.84 a barrel after a 0.81% gain the week before. Brent crude futures expiring in December rose 4.91% this week, hovering around $109.69 a barrel after a 2.42% increase the week before.

The United States Oil Fund ETF (USO) rose about 3% on Friday, while the ProShares Ultra Bloomberg Crude Oil ETF (UCO) gained more than 4%.

During the after-hours session on Friday, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), which tracks the S&P 500 index, fell 0.26%; the Invesco QQQ Trust ETF (QQQ) edged lower by 0.27%; and the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) declined 0.21%. Retail sentiment on Stocktwits toward the S&P 500 ETF was in the ‘bearish’ territory at the time of writing.

data.title: India bars sugarcane juice, syrup-based ethanol in 2026-27 tender; OMCs seek 1,100 crore litres
data.description:
India has barred oil marketing companies (OMCs) from procuring ethanol made from sugarcane juice, sugar, sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses for the 2026-27 ethanol supply year, with the government directing that sugar diversion for ethanol be reduced to zero.

The restriction is set out in a quantity bid tender dated October 16, issued by five state-run oil companies for the supply of around 1,100 crore litres of denatured anhydrous ethanol between November 1, 2026, and October 31, 2027.

The tender allows procurement from C-heavy molasses, damaged food grains, surplus rice sourced from the Food Corporation of India (FCI), maize and other eligible feedstocks under the National Policy on Biofuels. The move comes amid concerns over domestic sugar availability and prices.

The participating companies are Indian Oil Corporation, Bharat Petroleum Corporation, Hindustan Petroleum Corporation, Mangalore Refinery and Petrochemicals and Numaligarh Refinery.

Corn, rice and damaged food grains among eligible feedstocks

The tender specifies different procurement rates depending on the feedstock. Ethanol made from maize has a basic rate of ₹66.07 per litre, with an additional incentive of ₹2.79 per litre, excluding Goods and Services Tax (GST).

The basic procurement rate for ethanol made from damaged food grains is ₹64 per litre, while surplus rice procured from FCI carries a rate of ₹60.32 per litre. Ethanol made from C-heavy molasses has a basic rate of ₹57.97 per litre.

Transportation charges and applicable GST are payable over and above the basic rates. Ethanol made from other eligible feedstocks under the National Policy on Biofuels will be procured at the lowest prevailing rate under the tender.

The tender covers four supply quarters, running from November 2026 to January 2027, February to April 2027, May to July 2027, and August to October 2027. However, offers for ethanol made from surplus FCI rice will not be accepted for the fourth quarter.

Allocations subject to pending court proceedings

The tender also states that ethanol allocations under the first quarter of the 2026-27 supply year will remain subject to the outcome of pending legal proceedings concerning the OMCs’ ethanol allocation methodology.

The companies have reserved the right to revise, reduce, withdraw or cancel allocations in line with court orders, without liability for compensation to suppliers.

The tender requires suppliers to offer ethanol produced from eligible indigenous feedstocks at their own registered or approved distilleries. Trading or sourcing ethanol from third parties for onward supply to the OMCs is not permitted.

The restrictions apply to procurement under this tender for the 2026-27 supply year, which begins on November 1.

data.title: Greenpeace activists occupy Woodside gas project unit off Western Australia
data.description:
Greenpeace said on Saturday activists occupied a floating production unit at Woodside's $12.5 billion Scarborough gas project off the coast of Western Australia state.

  • Four activists scaled the unit and displayed banners with message "Stop Woodside’s Dirty Gas. Save Scott Reef", the environmental advocacy group said on its website. The protest temporarily shut down operations at the semi-submersible unit, Greenpeace said.

  • Greenpeace is among environmental groups concerned about the project's potential impact on Scott Reef, a coral system and foraging area for the endangered pygmy blue whale located about 390 km (242 miles) off the state's northwest coast.

  • Woodside in a statement said it was "responding to an incident involving individuals who have gained unlawful access to the Scarborough floating production unit".

  • "Our immediate focus is on managing the situation safely and minimising risk to the individuals involved and our workforce," a Woodside spokesperson said.

  • Australian Border Force said it was aware of protest activity off the Western Australian coast and was working with federal and state agencies in response.

  • Woodside says it has conducted extensive environmental consultation on the project since 2018.

data.title: ECB's Rehn says staying vigilant to risk of second-round inflation effects
data.description:
European Central Bank policymaker Olli Rehn said on Saturday that policymakers would stay vigilant to the risk of second-round inflation effects from higher energy prices as they might creep in quietly.

"There is no sign of second-round effects, but we will stay vigilant because they might creep in quietly," the Finnish central bank chief said at an event in Bangkok.

data.title: Strong dollar, weak hand for Trump before midterms: McGeever
data.description:
By Jamie McGeever

With the US midterm elections weeks away, a surging dollar is exposing a central contradiction in President Donald Trump's economic agenda: currency markets are delivering the opposite of what his administration wants.

Trump's economic record in the first two years of his second term is being heavily scrutinized. Polls show voters' approval of his handling of the economy has rarely been lower. That goes a long way toward explaining why betting markets point to his Republican Party losing control of the House of Representatives, and perhaps even the Senate, on November 3.

Yet if there's any truth to the market adage that a country's currency is a reflection of the world's confidence in its economy, Trump should be going into the upcoming vote brimming with confidence. The dollar has been rising steadily, recently hitting its strongest level in 18 months against major peers.

But a strong and appreciating exchange rate is the last thing Trump wants. His administration's economic and trade policies are aiming to revive US manufacturing, make American exports great again and shrink the trade deficit. A strengthening currency won't help with any of that.

WRONG DIRECTION

One might expect the dollar to be under pressure, especially given that the US trade balance has not narrowed according to the administration's plan. Imports have exploded to record levels, largely driven by US companies hoovering up the chips, equipment and goods needed for the AI build-out, and the country's trade deficit is widening. It was 2.7% of gross domestic product earlier this year — one of the smallest readings of the century — but it could be headed for 4% of GDP next year, according to Dean Maki at hedge fund Point72.

But the dollar is not weakening. It did during Trump's first year back in the Oval Office, amid concerns about "dollar debasement" and a "sell America" mentality among foreign investors fostered by Trump's tariffs, but that has since gone into reverse.

Why? Because exchange rates are relative, and the greenback currently appears to be the proverbial "cleanest dirty shirt." While the US is suffering from acute debt and deficit concerns, so are other developed countries, most notably France. Investors fear that Paris is unwilling to take the politically unpalatable steps to get its budget under control and are thus slamming the euro .

Similarly, worries that higher interest rates will make it nearly impossible for Japan to service its enormous debt load have anchored the yen near its recent historical lows.

In short, the dollar is "winning" as much by default as it is benefiting from the flood of global capital chasing the US AI dream.

This is not what the White House had in mind.

Trump and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent clearly want a weaker dollar, even if decades of a quasi-official "strong dollar" policy at the White House — dating back to the days of former Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin in the 1990s — make it challenging for them to say so outright.

The Trump administration's views on the US currency were flagged almost exactly two years ago in "A User’s Guide to Restructuring the Global Trading System," a paper by Stephen Miran, then a senior strategist at hedge fund Hudson Bay Capital Management.

Miran went on to serve as chairman of the Council of Economic Advisers under Trump, who later appointed him as a Federal Reserve governor for a short spell. He has since returned to HBC, but his 41-page manual still appears to serve as a broad framework for the administration's trade, currency and economic policy.

The blueprint has come to be known as the "Mar-a-Lago Accord," in a nod to the famous 1985 "Plaza Accord," under which the world's leading economic powers agreed to devalue the dollar.

Echoing Trump's decades-long view, Miran wrote that "deep unhappiness with the prevailing economic order is rooted in persistent overvaluation of the dollar ... (which) makes US exports less competitive, US imports cheaper, and handicaps American manufacturing."

He has a point. At the time of Trump's inauguration in January last year, the dollar's broad, real effective exchange rate was the strongest in over 30 years.

Miran argues that the global trade and financial systems can be rewired to America's benefit, but the path "is narrow, and will require careful planning, precise execution, and attention to steps to minimize adverse consequences."

Americans casting their midterm election votes on November 3 may not have the patience for this. While the US economy continues to grow at a healthy pace and unemployment remains low, households are feeling the adverse economic consequences of Trump's policies over the past two years.

Tariffs have raised the cost of imported goods, according to a recent New York Fed study, and the US war with Iran, launched in February, has led to soaring energy costs, most notably record-high diesel prices at the pump. As a consequence, inflation remains elevated, bond yields are the highest in a quarter of a century, and real wages are now falling.

Given all this, the big question is whether the American public will give the Trump administration the space to try to turn the dollar's tide.

A FAREWELL TO MULTILATERALISM

Efforts to reverse the dollar's march higher will be challenging, to put it mildly. History suggests that what's needed is multilateral, globally coordinated action, but that is the antithesis of Trump's "America First" worldview.

Piecemeal and bilateral actions, like the Treasury's recent intervention with Japan to support the yen , are likely too small to have any lasting impact.

Further interventions cannot be ruled out if the dollar continues to strengthen.

For example, when writing about the yen, Stephen Jen, CEO of Eurizon SLJ Asset Management, recently argued that a series of targeted, surprise "mini" interventions could chip away at the dollar without triggering an avalanche of depreciation, helping the Trump administration meet its foreign exchange and wider goals over time.

"The Trump Administration ... wants to find ways to guide the dollar lower. This is needed because, in order for the US to attain economic security, it needs to reclaim a certain level of manufacturing self-sufficiency. To do that, a weaker dollar would be necessary. The challenge, of course, is to guide the dollar lower without spooking the capital markets," Jen wrote in May.

Much will depend on the frequency and size of such moves. Official action to weaken the dollar against major currencies is rare. Before this year's yen intervention, the last time US and Japanese authorities coordinated to sell dollars against the yen was in 1998. The Fed intervened with the European Central Bank and other authorities to support the euro, but that was back in late 2000, just after the single currency's launch.

Since the era of free-floating exchange rates began in the early 1970s, when President Richard Nixon took the US off the gold standard, there have only been two truly global efforts to force a change in the dollar's broad value. Both were in the 1980s: the Plaza Accord in 1985 to lower what was an extremely elevated dollar, and the Louvre Accord in 1987 to essentially take the sting out of Plaza.

These accords were products of their time. The dollar is nowhere near as strong as it was back then, and that was an era when multilateral cooperation was still in vogue.

As the country looks set to enter the final two years of the Trump era, the dollar's relative strength could say much about how much of his economic agenda he has been able to achieve since first entering the White House almost 10 years ago.

(The opinions expressed here are those of the author, a columnist for Reuters)

data.title: Trump Denies Ordering Starlink Curbs in Ukraine, Says ‘It Wasn’t Me and I Don’t Think It Was Elon’ as Zelenskyy Warns Slower Speeds Put Lives at Risk
data.description:
President Donald Trump has denied ordering restrictions on Space Exploration Technologies Corp.’s satellite connectivity in Ukraine, as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says reduced speeds disrupted drone interceptions and other military operations.

Trump Denies Role in Starlink Restrictions

Speaking to reporters Friday, Trump rejected suggestions that he had directed the restrictions affecting Ukraine’s military access to Starlink and Starshield services, CNBC reported.

"I don’t know if it was anybody because it wasn’t me and I don’t think it was Elon," Trump said, adding that, to his knowledge, the service remained as it had been.

Ukrainian officials said earlier this week that the restrictions disrupted military operations without prior warning. Starshield is a military-focused satellite communications service that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk says the U.S. government owns and controls.

Musk pointed to Washington’s authority over the system, while Reuters reported, citing U.S. officials, that the White House made the decision to limit Starshield connectivity. The report did not identify who issued the order.

The Telegraph separately reported that Musk had approached Trump about slowing Starlink in Ukraine, alleging that both played a role in the restrictions.

SpaceX did not immediately respond to Benzinga’s request for comment.

Read Also: Trump’s $330 Million White House Ballroom Donor List Reveals Nvidia, Apple and Google Among Top Tech Contributors: Report

Zelenskyy Says Speed Cuts Hampered Drone Interceptions

Zelenskyy said Ukraine does not use Starlink for attacks inside Russia but relies on the technology to intercept Russian attack drones targeting civilians.

"Starlink wasn’t turned off — its speed was reduced," Zelenskyy said on X, explaining that the slowdown prevented Ukrainian forces from intercepting some jet-powered Shahed drones.

"We couldn’t use a tool that helps protect people. That’s very painful and frustrating," he added.

Zelenskyy also said the restrictions affected Ukrainian strikes against military targets in Russian-occupied territories and drone deliveries of food and water to troops stationed on the front lines.

He said connectivity had not fully returned to its previous performance levels, although restoration efforts were underway.

data.title: IDBI Bank sale: Legitimate employee concerns addressed, says MoS, Finance
data.description:
Legitimate concerns of the existing employees and other stakeholders of IDBI Bank have been suitably addressed through appropriate provisions made in the Share Purchase Agreement, according to Pankaj Chaudhary, Minister of State for Finance.

In a reply to an un-starred question in the Lok Sabha by Thamizhachi Thangapandian, the minister said Preliminary Information Memorandum for inviting Expression of Interest (EoI) from potential bidders was published on October 7, 2022. In response, multiple EOIs were received, due diligence of which is being undertaken after security clearance by Ministry of Home Affairs and ‘fit and proper ‘evaluation by the Reserve Bank of India.

Issues raised in House

The original question in the House pertained to current status of privatisation; whether specific assessments were done by Government to evaluate potential impact on officers of the bank; whether Government has any plans to discuss implications of the proposed privatisation with employees and their representatives.

Big lie, says United Forum

Meanwhile, the United Forum of IDBI Officers and Employees expressed shock over the statement by Arunish Chawla, Secretary, Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM), that it had discussed the disinvestment with employee associations. “We condemn the statement that DIPAM discussed the matter with representatives of the United Forum, the largest employee forum with 11,900 officers and 400 workmen employees as members. The United Forum was never consulted while preparing or finalising the draft of Share Purchase Agreement nor was its draft shared. The statement of Secretary, DIPAM, is a big lie,” it said

Dharnas, strike held

“We sat in dharna at Jantar Mantar, Delhi, on seven occasions opposing the proposed sale of the bank to private/foreign players. A memorandum was submitted to Secretary, DIPAM, opposing the proposed sale that went against interests of the nation as well as employees,” said Devidas Tuljapurkar, Convenor and Vithal Koteswara Rao and Ratnakar Wankhade, Joint Convenors, of the United Forum.

A one day nation-wide strike was observed on August 11, 2025. Several conciliation meetings were conducted before Assistant Labour Commissioner (Central), Mumbai, and Deputy Chief Labour Commissioner (Central), Mumbai, in 2025 and 2026. “DIPAM officials never discussed the matter with us; rather replied every time to Labour Commissioners that the strategic disinvestment is a policy decision of Government of India and is a confidential process,” they said.

Confidential process

Earlier last month, a senior DIPAM official wrote to Assistant Labour Commissioner-C (III), Mumbai, that the “strategic disinvestment is a confidential process, and contains price sensitive information akin to any sale and purchase transaction of a listed company that is required by regulation to be kept confidential. Any disclosure of terms of disinvestment would not only vitiate transparency and confidentiality of the bidding process but also be a breach by Government of confidentiality regulations and jeopardise disinvestment process altogether.“

The DIPAM observed that invoking of conciliation process amounts to no more than case of ‘forum-shopping,’ with the Supreme Court yet to decide on a similar plea and another one pending with Mumbai High Court.

data.title: Can the Russia Sanctions Bill waiver by Donald Trump bring more relief to Indian markets?
data.description:
US President Donald Trump’s decision to waive new sanctions and tariffs under America’s Russia sanctions law could provide some relief to Indian markets by removing an immediate source of uncertainty over the country’s purchases of Russian oil.

The Sensex and Nifty recorded their biggest weekly gains since the first week of April 2026, supported by a strong rebound in IT stocks. However, with crude prices surging amid escalating geopolitical tensions and Brent briefly crossing $110 a barrel on Friday, October 16, the outlook for equities remains closely tied to energy prices and global risk sentiment.

Trump, in an executive order dated October 16, waived the sanctions, restrictions and duties provided for under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, citing US national interests. The law had envisaged a 100% increase in duties on goods from the five largest importers of Russian-origin crude oil and natural gas if they knowingly made new purchases from October 18, subject to specified exceptions.

India, a major buyer of Russian crude, had faced potential exposure to the proposed tariffs. The waiver removes the immediate threat of these additional duties under the law while it remains in force, although it does not exempt India from other existing US tariffs or sanctions.

IT stocks lead recovery as AI concerns ease

Friday's gains extended the benchmark indices’ winning streak to a second consecutive week, taking their weekly advances to the highest level since the first week of April.

IT stocks were among the strongest drivers of the recovery, with Nifty IT index emerging as the best-performing sector last week. It rose nearly 12% to record its biggest weekly gain in 18 years. The index gained another 4% on Friday to close at 31,924, its highest level in eight months.

The rally added nearly $30 billion to the combined market capitalisation of the top 10 Indian IT companies during the week. Tata Consultancy Services accounted for $13.3 billion of the increase, while Infosys added around $7 billion and HCL Technologies saw its market value rise by $5.3 billion.

The rebound followed better-than-expected results from Indian software companies and a pullback in global AI-related stocks, helping revive investor confidence in the domestic IT sector. The rally also came after the Nifty IT index had been the worst-performing sectoral gauge this year until Wednesday.

The gains in IT stocks have helped lift the broader market, although the performance has been uneven across sectors. The Nifty FMCG index fell nearly 1% over the week, while the midcap index declined 67 points to close at 59,130 on Friday. The Bank Nifty ended marginally higher at 55,844.

Veteran investor and BSE member Ramesh Damani said: “I think we are witnessing the early stages of a major rotation in equity markets. The AI-led boom, which has largely overlooked India over the past few years, is now beginning to lose steam amid higher interest rates, stretched valuations and excessive exuberance.”

Crude prices remain a key risk

Despite the potential relief from the US waiver, the sharp rise in crude prices remains a concern for India, which depends heavily on imports to meet its oil requirements.

Brent crude crossed $110 a barrel on Friday for the first time since May before closing at $109.86. US benchmark West Texas Intermediate (WTI) settled above $101 a barrel, taking its weekly gain to around 10%. Brent rose more than 5% over the week.

Prices climbed as Iran escalated attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, Yemen’s Houthi rebels continued attacks affecting Saudi Arabia, and Ukraine vowed to continue targeting Russian energy infrastructure.

The conflict has raised concerns over the security of energy supplies and shipping routes. Although Russian crude exports have remained above recent lows, shipments for the week ended Wednesday stood at 9.4 million barrels per day, around 70% of pre-war levels, according to energy research firm Kpler.

data.title: Bitcoin ETFs post $82.39 million in net outflows as Ethereum funds shed $69.68 million
data.description:
US spot Bitcoin ETFs lost $82.39 million in net outflows on October 16. Their Ethereum counterparts had no better luck. They gave up $69.68 million the same day.

Combined, the two product groups saw roughly $152 million leave in one session.

The bigger picture is the monthly tally. Bitcoin ETFs had run up roughly $535 million in net outflows for October through mid-month. That reverses September, when the funds pulled in about $2.6 billion of fresh money.

Bitcoin ETF trading volume topped $7.5 billion in the week ending October 16. Net selling over the past week came to only about $145 million.

Not every count of the day matched. Alternative tallies put Bitcoin's daily outflow as low as $10.6 million, with Fidelity's FBTC leading the redemptions. Reporting differences between data sources are common with ETF flows, which settle and get compiled on different schedules.

Despite the recent selling, the Bitcoin ETF complex remains enormous. Total assets are estimated at around $105 to $106 billion. The funds collectively hold more than 1.27 million BTC.

Measured against those assets, the $82.39 million outflow is less than a tenth of one percent.

BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust, ticker IBIT, is the largest Bitcoin ETF by assets. Fidelity's FBTC and Grayscale's GBTC round out the most closely watched names. Grayscale's fund has a longer history than most, having converted from a closed-end trust into a spot ETF.

Ethereum ETFs are a smaller pond. They hold approximately $15 billion in total assets. That makes the $69.68 million daily outflow proportionally heavier than Bitcoin's, even though the dollar figure is lower.

Spot Bitcoin ETFs launched in the US in January 2024. Since then, cumulative net inflows have totaled roughly $57 billion.

Against that backdrop, October's roughly $535 million in outflows amounts to less than 1% of everything that has flowed in since launch.

Bitcoin is trading near $82,000. Ethereum sits between $2,400 and $2,500.

More than $7.5 billion in weekly trading against about $145 million in net selling suggests engagement has not disappeared. It has turned cautious.

The simultaneous outflows from both Bitcoin and Ethereum funds point toward a broader risk-off posture rather than a view on one specific asset.

For Ethereum, with a much smaller asset base of approximately $15 billion, sustained outflows of this size would take a bigger proportional bite than equivalent dollar outflows from Bitcoin ETFs.

The spread between an $82.39 million outflow and a $10.6 million one is wide enough to change the tone of a day's coverage. For anyone trading on flow data, knowing which source you rely on is half the battle.
